title: Draft Deposition Outline for Supervisor in Employment Discrimination and Retaliation Case

blind.coverage: Read task.json in full: the instructions and all 59 criteria. Read all 12 supplied documents in full: the first amended complaint, the HR investigation report, the PIP, the 2023 review, the termination letter, the Whitford-Cho chain, the Q4 email, the IT ticket, the SVP spreadsheet, the discrimination complaint email, and the Whitford/Yazzie personnel file. The EEO policy was searched rather than read end to end, covering §7.4.1-7.4.4, 7.5, 7.6, 7.7, 7.8 and the acknowledgment form. Read the solver system prompt and the judge prompt. The judge sees no documents and gets no leniency guidance, and the system prompt does not name the solver's client. Checked the arithmetic against the spreadsheet (averages of 2.6% and $38.7M) and the calendar (2024 is a leap year). No legal proposition in the rubric needed a defect finding. The Kolstad and cat's-paw framing matches settled law as I understand it, but I did not pull the primary texts, so no authorities are listed as verified. Not verified: how the two judges actually treat the timestamp and track-record wording.

findings.title: Criteria hardcode a '4:47 PM' Q4 submission time; the email header reads 04:47 -0000
findings.explanation: The '4:47 PM' time and the '5:00 PM COB' deadline come only from the complaint (FAC ¶60). The exhibit's header reads 04:47 in 24-hour format with a -0000 zone. That is 4:47 AM UTC, which is 9:47 PM MST on January 9. The Whitford-Cho chain uses an explicit -0700, so this does not look like an extraction artifact. The review says only that the report was 'due January 10, 2024.' Either reading puts the submission before the deadline, so the impeachment point stands. But C-009's PASS text requires the email 'with its 4:47 PM timestamp,' and the judge cannot see the exhibit. A careful outline that quotes the real header, or flags the conflict with the complaint (a prudent step before impeaching with it), could be failed. C-008's '4:47 PM, before the 5:00 PM COB deadline' has the same risk, though less sharply.

evidence.quote: via email to Whitford on January 10, 2024, at 4:47 PM. The established deadline for Q4 quarterly risk reports was close of business (5:00 PM)
The Q4 2023 risk report, due January 10, 2024, was submitted 5 business days late
references the Q4 risk report submission email (q4-risk-report-email.eml) with its 4:47 PM timestamp

findings.suggested_fix: Tie C-009 to the email's showing that it was submitted on January 10 or earlier, before the deadline. Drop the hardcoded '4:47 PM', or accept any accurate reading of the header.

findings.title: The '8 of 10 Exceeds' figure counts 2023 as Exceeds; the record shows 2023 was Meets (7 of 10)
findings.explanation: C-054 names the complaint's figure of 'Exceeds Expectations' on 8 of 10 reviews. That count depends on FAC ¶12-13 listing 2023 as 'Exceeds.' The 2023 review, spreadsheet cell R3, and FAC ¶35-36 itself all show 2023 as 'Meets.' The HR report's table shows 7 Exceeds in 9 reviews through 2022. The correct figure is therefore 7 of 10. The criterion rewards putting a number to Whitford that he could correctly deny. It could also make a judge doubt an outline that states the accurate '7 of 9' or '7 of 10.' The 'or substantially equivalent reference to her track record' clause probably saves accurate answers, so this is arguable rather than problematic.

findings.suggested_fix: Ask for a reference to her strong prior record, for example Exceeds in 7 of 9 reviews through 2022 and three Exceeds ratings under Whitford. Do not require the '8 of 10' figure.

findings.title: Requires explicit notes on open-ended vs. leading questions, a meta-annotation the instructions never ask for
findings.explanation: The instructions ask only for 'a deposition outline.' A competent outline shows question technique by using open narrative questions and tight leading sequences. It does not usually annotate when to use each form. Leading an adverse party's managing agent is routine, so the substance is fine. The hidden element is requiring written guidance about question form rather than the questions themselves. Two strong outlines, one with and one without such meta-notes, would score differently for no difference in usefulness. Under the all-pass metric, that alone can zero a run.

evidence.quote: PASS if the outline includes at least some notes or guidance about when to use open-ended questions ... versus leading/closed questions
Prepare a deposition outline for the plaintiff's former supervisor using the attached case file and exhibits.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete C-049, or pass any outline that clearly uses both open and leading question sequences where they fit.

findings.title: Requires an emotional-distress damages section in the liability supervisor's deposition outline
findings.explanation: Whitford is the liability and motive witness. Emotional-distress damages are normally built through the plaintiff, treating providers, and family. A competent outline that stays on discrimination, retaliation, pretext, comparators, policy, and punitive-damages foundation, which other criteria already require, could reasonably leave out damages questions for this witness. A few questions about her reaction at the termination meeting are a sensible optional topic, not an implicit part of a supervisor outline. Making them mandatory under all-pass can fail otherwise complete work.

evidence.quote: FAIL if emotional distress/compensatory damages are not addressed at all.

findings.suggested_fix: Drop C-059 or make it non-gating. At most, fold it into a general 'termination meeting' topic.

findings.title: Instructions never name the client; the rubric assumes plaintiff's counsel is taking the deposition
findings.explanation: The instructions say only 'a deposition outline for the plaintiff's former supervisor.' The system prompt adds no role. The rubric is written entirely from the taking side: lock-in before confronting him with the email, impeachment, target admissions, and malice/reckless-indifference admissions. The most natural reading of 'deposition outline for [adverse witness]' is a taking outline, so most competent solvers will choose that side. A solver who read it as defense counsel's outline for preparing its own witness (a real work product for a supervisor defendant's counsel would prepare) would fail these criteria wholesale. The risk is real but limited, so this is arguable.

evidence.quote: Prepare a deposition outline for the plaintiff's former supervisor using the attached case file and exhibits.
questions designed to establish that Whitford acted with malice or reckless indifference to Delgado-Reyes's protected rights

findings.suggested_fix: State in the instructions that the solver represents plaintiff and is taking Whitford's deposition.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tied to the record. It gets the comparator figures right (Langley 3.1%/$36.1M/$4.7M, Kowalski 2.8%/$39.4M, division averages 2.6% and $38.7M). The PIP end date (March 21) and the 7-day early termination check out. So do the IT ticket's extension, the §7.4.1 90-day approval rule, the Yazzie file, and Cho's 'open investigation' remark after the February 12 closure. The Kolstad and cat's-paw framing is correctly stated, and no criterion states wrong law. The defects found are all arguable, not problematic: two criteria hardcode record facts that only the complaint supports and the exhibits contradict (C-009's '4:47 PM', C-054's '8 of 10'); two gating criteria demand optional content (C-049 question-form meta-notes, C-059 damages via the supervisor); and the instructions never name the client. Record issues that do not change any criterion: the HR report says the 2023 review was not final as of February 12, but the review is dated February 5. The complaint's '65 days' is really 66 because 2024 is a leap year, and C-022 requires no count. FAC ¶36's 'first Meets under Whitford' is contradicted by his 2021 Meets rating. C-040 quotes the complaint's paraphrase rather than §7.4.1's text, but PASS turns on substance. The spreadsheet shows Trujillo (Hispanic, rated Below Expectations, $22.9M, no PIP), the strongest defense fact against the comparator theory; the rubric neither requires nor penalizes addressing him. With 59 all-pass criteria, many of them exhibit-reference or number-specific checks, the rubric is demanding, but most of what it asks is implicit in a thorough plaintiff-side taking outline.

sol_verdicts.reason: I re-checked the exhibit. Its header reads 'Wed, 10 Jan 2024 04:47:00 -0000', which is 24-hour UTC and so 9:47 PM Phoenix time on January 9. The other .eml files use -0700, so this is how the exhibit was written, not an extraction artifact. C-009 credits the email itself with a '4:47 PM timestamp', which misstates the exhibit, so it is problematic. C-008 only cites 4:47 PM in a parenthetical, and its PASS condition turns on challenging timeliness with the evidence, so it is arguable. Either reading makes the report timely.

FAC ¶12 counts 2023 as Exceeds to reach '8 of 10'. FAC ¶35-36, the 2023 review ('3 --- Meets Expectations') and spreadsheet R3 all show Meets. The HR table shows 7 Exceeds in 9 reviews through 2022. So the criterion names a count the record contradicts. Its 'or substantially equivalent reference to her track record' clause should still pass accurate answers, which keeps this arguable rather than confirmed.

C-038 only requires questions that pin Whitford to the reasons stated in the PIP and termination letter, which is standard pretext practice. Under McKennon, after-acquired evidence limits remedies, not liability. Locking in that the stated reasons were the only contemporaneous reasons is exactly what stops the employer from later recasting misconduct discovered afterwards as a real motive. The parenthetical is loose shorthand, it does not require any wrong legal statement, and it would not misgrade an outline.

Sequencing notes (C-048), holding the smoking-gun email until testimony is locked in (C-006), and target admissions (C-050) are standard parts of a taking deposition outline, and each FAIL condition applies only when they are entirely absent. That makes them implicit, not hidden. C-049 is different: it demands written meta-guidance on question form, which a good outline shows by its questions rather than annotates. C-006 and C-050 are separately arguable only on the unnamed-client ground, covered in finding O6.

findings.title: C-009 credits the Q4 email with a '4:47 PM timestamp', but its header reads 04:47 -0000 (9:47 PM Phoenix time on Jan 9)
findings.explanation: '4:47 PM' and the 5:00 PM COB deadline come only from FAC ¶60. The exhibit C-009 names shows 'Wed, 10 Jan 2024 04:47:00 -0000'. RFC 2822 headers use 24-hour time, so that is 4:47 AM UTC, or 9:47 PM MST on January 9. The Whitford-Cho chain and the complaint email use explicit -0700, so the exhibit was written this way. C-009 therefore states a false fact about the exhibit and rewards repeating it. A careful examiner would quote the real header or flag the conflict with the complaint before impeaching Whitford with it; getting the time wrong invites rehabilitation. Such an outline falls between C-009's PASS condition (the '4:47 PM timestamp') and its FAIL condition (the email not referenced), and a literal judge who cannot see the exhibit may fail it. Either reading still makes the report timely.

evidence.quote: via email to Whitford on January 10, 2024, at 4:47 PM. The established deadline for Q4 quarterly risk reports was close of business (5:00 PM)
references the Q4 risk report submission email (q4-risk-report-email.eml) with its 4:47 PM timestamp

findings.suggested_fix: Require that the email be used to show the report was submitted on or before January 10, the due date, and so was not five business days late. Drop the hardcoded '4:47 PM', or fix the exhibit header to 16:47 -0700.

findings.title: C-008's parenthetical ('4:47 PM, before the 5:00 PM COB deadline') repeats the complaint's time, which the exhibit contradicts
findings.explanation: C-008's PASS condition turns on challenging the PIP's claim that the report was late and planning to introduce evidence that it was on time. The '4:47 PM ... 5:00 PM COB' detail sits in a parenthetical. It comes from FAC ¶60 and conflicts with the exhibit header, which works out to 9:47 PM Phoenix time on January 9. The 2023 review says only 'due January 10, 2024.' Most judges will grade on substance, but a literal one might mark down an outline that gives the correct header time or notes the discrepancy. That is less likely than for C-009, so this is arguable.

evidence.quote: references or plans to introduce evidence that it was actually submitted on time (January 10, 2024, at 4:47 PM, before the 5:00 PM COB deadline)
The Q4 2023 risk report, due January 10, 2024, was submitted 5 business days late

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the parenthetical with 'submitted on or before the January 10, 2024 due date', or accept any accurate reading of the email header.

The criterion rewards putting a count to Whitford that he could correctly deny. The 'substantially equivalent reference to her track record' clause should rescue an outline that gives the accurate 7 of 9 or 7 of 10, so the risk of misgrading is modest.

findings.title: C-049 requires explicit notes on open-ended vs. leading questions, a meta-annotation the instructions never ask for
findings.explanation: The instructions ask only for 'a deposition outline.' A competent outline shows its technique through the questions themselves: open narrative questions on background, tight leading chains on damaging facts. It does not usually add prose explaining when to use each form. Unlike sequencing (C-048) or target admissions (C-050), which are standard parts of a taking outline, this is guidance about writing questions rather than part of the work product. Two equally useful outlines can differ only in whether they carry such notes, and under the all-pass metric this one criterion can zero a run.

findings.title: The instructions never name the client, but the rubric assumes plaintiff's counsel is taking the deposition
findings.explanation: The instructions say only 'a deposition outline for the plaintiff's former supervisor', and the system prompt assigns no role. The rubric is written wholly from the taking side: lock-in before confronting him with the email, impeachment with documents, target admissions, and malice or reckless-indifference admissions. The most natural reading is a plaintiff-side taking outline, so most competent solvers will land there. But the file includes internal Ridgeline documents, and defense counsel preparing its own supervisor-witness is real work. A solver who took that reading would fail these criteria wholesale. The risk is real but limited.

final.changes_from_blind: I split blind O1 in two after re-checking the record and reading Sol. C-009 is now problematic (O1): it says the email itself has a '4:47 PM timestamp', but the exhibit's 24-hour UTC header rules that out, which meets the 'states wrong facts' prong. C-008 stays arguable (O2) because its PASS condition turns on substance and the time appears only in a parenthetical. I kept C-054 arguable rather than following Sol's 'confirmed', because the equivalence clause rescues accurate answers. I rejected Sol's C-038 finding: its after-acquired-evidence parenthetical is consistent with McKennon and requires nothing wrong. I rejected Sol's unrequested-requirement theory for C-006, C-048 and C-050, since sequencing, lock-in before the exhibit, and target admissions are standard parts of a taking outline. C-006 and C-050 remain arguable only under the unnamed-client finding (O6). Blind findings O3 (C-049), O4 (C-059) and O5 (client role) are kept unchanged and renumbered O4, O5 and O6. No blind finding was dropped.
final.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tied to the record: the comparator figures, the PIP dates, the early termination, the IT ticket, §7.4.1, the Yazzie file and the Cho emails all check out. One criterion is problematic. C-009 credits the Q4 email with a '4:47 PM timestamp' that the exhibit's header (04:47 -0000) contradicts; that time comes only from the complaint. The rest are arguable. C-008 repeats the same time in a parenthetical. C-054 names the complaint's internally inconsistent '8 of 10 Exceeds' count, though an equivalence clause softens it. C-049 (question-form meta-notes) and C-059 (damages through the liability supervisor) require optional content under an all-pass metric. And the instructions never say which side the solver represents, though the rubric assumes plaintiff's counsel. No criterion states wrong law; Sol's McKennon concern about C-038 does not hold up.
final.coverage: This pass re-read the 11 criteria at issue (C-006, C-008, C-009, C-038, C-045, C-047 through C-050, C-054, C-059) and the instructions. I re-checked the Q4 email header against the other .eml headers, which use -0700. I checked every 'Exceeds' and '4:47' reference in the complaint, the HR report, the 2023 review, the PIP and the spreadsheet, and the complaint's 2023 downgrade allegations (¶12, ¶35-38). I read Sol's audit .md and index entry; Sol's .json is the same content. The blind pass covered all 59 criteria and all 12 documents. McKennon and Kolstad are cited from knowledge, not read in this session, so no authority is marked verified.
